newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Gritty Bhutto vows to fight her dismissal.
newsitem.headline: Gritty Bhutto vows to fight her dismissal.

text.p: Scathing and indignant by turns, Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto fought back on Wednesday, vowing to ask the courts to overturn her dismissal by her former political ally President Farooq Leghari.
Appearing in public for the first time since Leghari sacked her early on Tuesday, Bhutto told a crowded news conference that she was the victim of a conspiracy to smear her name.
"Lies, lies, lies," she said of allegations that her three-year government had let corruption run riot, undermined the judiciary and allowed the security forces to kill at will.
The 43-year-old mother of three accused Leghari of arranging the abduction of her husband Asif Ali Zardari, who is in what the new government has called "protective custody".
She threatened to bring a kidnapping charge against Leghari unless her lawyer was granted immediate access to Zardari, and handed out copies of a letter she had written to the president.
"I believe that my husband...has been kidnapped on your orders," the handwritten letter said. "You have taken an oath to adhere to the law. This is not being done."

Bhutto, wearing a white headscarf, received reporters at the prime minister's elegant official residence in Islamabad, where she was confined after her dismissal. New Information Minister Irshad Haqqani said curbs on her had been lifted on Wednesday.
Bhutto blasted Leghari, whom she nominated for president after her October 1993 election victory.
"He has no vision, he is no great strategist, but he is a good implementer," she said of a man long regarded as a loyal supporter of her Pakistan People's Party (PPP).
Bhutto said Leghari had broken his "solemn pledge" not to dismiss an elected government. "He had no right to do this," she thundered. "I leave his fate in Allah's hands."
She announced plans to challenge her dismissal in the Supreme Court, which reinstated the government of her rival Nawaz Sharif after he was sacked by a former president in 1993.
"We expect the court to restore the (National) Assembly within a month," she declared. "I have been elected as prime minister and I'll be prime minister again."
Leghari, accusing Bhutto's government of corruption and misrule, dissolved the assembly on Tuesday and appointed an interim government to oversee elections in February,
Bhutto described the president's charges as "malicious, baseless and fabricated" and called on him to resign if he wanted to prove he had not acted out of a "lust for power".
She likened her old ally to a guilt-ridden Shakespearean character, saying: "For the rest of his life, he's going to be like Lady Macbeth, saying 'Out, damned spot'."

Bhutto, who has tasted jail fare as well as state banquets in her turbulent political career, said the killing of her brother Murtaza by Karachi police on September 20 was a pre-meditated conspiracy to destabilise democracy.
"The bullet that was meant to kill my brother physically was meant to destroy me politically. It was a conspiracy against the Bhutto family," she said. "We've lost all our male members."
Her father Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, Pakistan's first popularly elected prime minister, was overthrown in a military coup in 1977 and hanged on a contested murder conviction in 1979.
Her younger brother Shahnawaz died in mysterious circumstances in France in 1985, apparently of poisoning.
She was estranged from Murtaza, who had set up a rival faction of the PPP their father founded, but his killing dealt her a devastating personal blow.
Bhutto, who clawed her way back to power in 1993 after being sacked a first time in 1990, vowed to make another comeback.
"Whenever I've given a call, the people of Pakistan have never deserted me," she said. "I think I've done a fine job as prime minister and only the people and my God have the right to judge me."
